# Designing the Study {background-image="assets/symbol_study.png" background-opacity="0.3" background-size="cover" background-color="#2d4059"}

A benchmark is only as good as the instances it runs on.

## Exploratory vs. workhorse studies

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Exploratory** — fast, cheap, throwaway.

- few instances, short limits.
- Build intuition, kill bad ideas early.
- Conclusions are *hypotheses*, not results.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Workhorse** — large, rigorous, reproducible.

- Curated instance set, fixed seeds, pinned environment.
- The numbers you put in a paper or a deploy decision.
:::
::::

::: {.platypus-warning}
The classic failure: Not clearly distinguishing the two. Don't just "iterate" an exploratory study until it feels like a workhorse study.
:::

## Selecting the instance set, and managing the runs

- **Instance set:** representative of production, spanning sizes; include hard cases, not just the solvable ones. Beware homogeneous generators that hide the no-free-lunch effect.
- **Reproducibility:** allow others to rerun your study.
- **Log everything:** there will be outliers and Heisenbugs; you can only debug on the data you saved.
- **Folder discipline:** `evaluations/<problem>/<date_tag>/` with `PRIVATE_DATA` + `PUBLIC_DATA`, a `README`, numbered scripts (`00_generate`, `01_run`, …).
- **Make runs observable, interruptible & resumable** — the longer the runs, the higher the risk of system failures.
